body.input: Jane, Jane, you’ll never guess what black bears do in autumn—
Eat a lot? I’ve seen you at a buffet, Paul.
They enter hyperphagia! Twenty thousand calories a day, twenty hours of foraging, berries, nuts, acorns—
That fat is their only fuel for months, yes. And when food runs out, usually between October and December, they den up.
A hollow tree, a cave, even a hole in a hillside—
Snow isn’t needed, but it does insulate the den.
Then comes the magic: no eating, no drinking, no bathroom breaks for months.
Heart rate drops from fifty beats to eight, and they breathe once every forty-five seconds. Almost like you after a big lunch.
And their body temperature barely drops! So they can wake up fast if disturbed.
They can still lose fifteen to thirty percent of their body weight.
But here’s the sweet part: cubs are born in January or February, tiny, blind, almost hairless, nursing while mum’s still hibernating.
And the family leaves the den between March and May.
Not every bear hibernates, though. If food’s available all winter, some stay active.
And polar bears? Only the pregnant females den for winter.
Until next time, keep it wild.
